utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, you are to continue with your cross-examination. Before you do so, let me say that, regrettably, Judge Fassi Fihri is still indisposed. Judge May and I will continue in accordance with the provisions of Rule 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you looked at a number of establishments which related to the running the Keraterm camp, and in particular, you looked at some documents that led you to conclude that it was the Crisis Staff that established the camp. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the tasks of security and interrogation of inmates were delegated, if I could use that word, to the Prijedor Police Station. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, because the interrogation of persons who were in Keraterm camp was given to combined teams of highly professional personnel, which were the state security police officers, the Banja Luka Corps military team, and the Banja Luka Security Services Centres, but I agree with you that the Prijedor II police station did get the task of interrogating these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you looked at a number of documents from which you concluded that there was a hierarchical structure at the Prijedor Police Station. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And that includes the commander of the police station for the security facilities, deputy, two assistants, the officer of duty, and everything else I mentioned. These would be lower-ranking police tasks and activities that pertain to this station, such as the role of drivers and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And can you just clarify, please, which documents you looked at in order to derive that conclusion? You referred in your report to the duty rosters for the 5th and 6th of June, 1992, which are Exhibits D41/1 and D42/1 in these proceedings. Were they the documents that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you did not mention one very important bylaw, which is a rule of internal organisation, which is -- which covers the maintenance of law and order, and there it says that the commander of the police station for the security of public facilities also controls and commands the police station. Then he controls the implementation of tasks on the part of security, that is, persons who are engaged in security tasks, that is, security facilities and persons, assigns tasks, and monitors the implementation of legal provisions, and in case of any violations, prosecutes it, and disciplinary measures. He is also responsible for the law and order in the station. This provision is completely adopted from the rules of the internal organisation and systematisation of the job classification of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and during the wartime it was applied by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republika Srpska. I assert here with full responsibility, because I also gave evidence in the Prcac case in Omarska, that there are only four types of ranks in this police station. It's under 28, commander; under 35, deputy commander; two assistants under 38; and the policemen under 53 for security of facilities and persons. It is very interesting to see what the conditions or what the requirements are for a police officer to be employed for security facilities. He has to have had a four-year police schooling or some equivalent --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just, can I just stop you there? You've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The point is that it was the duty rosters from the 5th and 6th of June, 1992, that is, Exhibit D41/2 and Exhibit D42/1, from what you looked at to conclude that there was a hierarchical structure in Prijedor at the Prijedor police station; that's right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a copy of Exhibit D41/1 and D42/1 with you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the duty roster?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes, for the 5th and 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: All right. Sir, now, can you point that document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, it appears, Doctor, that the copy you have been shown is equally as difficult to read as the copy that I have. Can you tell me where it is in that document that the precise roles are set out, that is, for the commander, the deputy commander, and the assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be superfluous because the activities and tasks of the commander of the police station, his deputy, and his assistants, and even police officers who are on security tasks, are defined by the rules on internal organisation and job classification of the Republika Srpska, that is, the previous rules of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, this duty roster would, would be superfluous; in other words, it would be superfluous to identify these jobs. But there is -- something else is important. If you look at the patrolman or people on security tasks, there would be a patrol duty roster, an order in which the commander, his deputy or assistants would assist for a particular day, which special particular tasks are to be executed, and when the shift is over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The question was, where in the document is it set out. Is the answer, it isn't set out in the document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end, it states "Commander, Deputy Commander, and Assistant Commanders," and then there are signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The point is, nowhere in that document does it specify exactly what the roles of those persons who occupied those positions are. It doesn't set that out in that document, does it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But there is no need for it either. I don't know if you understand me. I wonder if you would just follow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just try to -- to interpret what you've said. What you've done is applied the regulations as you understand them to this document, and you have assumed that the roles were the same. That's what you've done, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: That document itself does not -- is specific to the police station. It's not specific to Keraterm camp. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Keraterm camp is emergency security of -- facility, and when you talk about the emergency or extraordinary security, that means that a plan of security is drawn up for that, and all the rules which are set out in these rules of internal organisation, all its provisions are implemented within that plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The point is that that document refers very generally to the roles of the police at any other station, that is, at the hospital, at Keraterm, at the post office, at the bank. Any other station is just referred to very generally in that document; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I said, and please try to accept it, that for each facility there has to be a security plan in which a commander will define the security situation, the number of policemen engaged, the shifts, either 12- or 24-hour shifts, the way of the policemen's arrival at work, their leaving work, the communication lines and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The point is, you have not seen such a plan for Keraterm camp. You are assuming that it must have existed. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct. And I did not see it. But the rules on the public security in Articles 142 to 146 expressly provides that the leader of -- the top official has to provide a plan of security and has to notify the personnel involved in security about their tasks and activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So if the rules say that this must be done, you are assuming that it was done; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a realistic and logical line of reasoning and that is also my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In any event, that document, the duty roster for the police station, is the document that you realise upon in order to conclude that there was no hierarchical structure at the Keraterm camp. Now, can you answer that yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, if we read your evidence and your report together, you have concluded from the document, that is, the duty roster for the 5th and 6th of June, 1992, that -- you've concluded from that document that there was no hierarchical structure at Keraterm camp. That's what you've concluded; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this, if I may say - and I'm just expanding and elaborating now - as of 26, I was able to review some additional documents and that the rules of internal organisation and job classification is silent about the -- either the shift commander, which is what the accused Dosen is alleged to have been, and the accused Kolundzija. And I also assert here with full responsibility that the official note which you showed me -- I have to apologise to the Trial Chamber here and to you, Madam Prosecutor, and also to the Defence counsel. On Thursday when you showed me this official note, I had been giving evidence for five hours and I was quite exhausted at the end of that, and due to my full -- due to my health and my age, I said that I did not use it, but I did use it you can say -- we can see in page 5, line 4 of my expert finding and opinion. And now I am prepared to tell you and I'm prepared to answer in regard of the accused Dosen and in the case of the accused Kolundzija and the accused Sikirica that they could not have been, in the case of Sikirica, chief of security, and that the others could not have been shift commanders, and I'm prepared to give full explanation about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, I think you have, sir, and just let me try and summarise. What you've said is because the rules are silent, because the rules do not refer to the term "shift commander," that that position did not exist. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have two additional arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, would you just answer the question as simply and as shortly as possible. We do have another phase in the examination: re-examination, when your counsel would be in a position to ask you for further explanations. So would you answer the question as precisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your warning. But my position and my opinion is based on the subrules which regulates the organisation and job classification, and that one is silent on those two jobs, those two duties: the shift commander and the chief of security. That's argument number one, the first piece of evidence that I can cite. Also, my practical experience which I have had at the Institute of State Security in the former SFRY when, as a member of a team, I travelled to correctional centres around Yugoslavia and had an opportunity to see and to hear when a guard in a correctional centre permits a convict to light a cigarette or go to the canteen, that he addresses him as, "Thank you, Commander," even though he is a simple guard. That means that this act of goodwill, small as it may be but big enough for a convict, is translated into a commander rather than guard because the guard could be considered too low, perhaps. Also, the third argument that also contributed to my position both in terms of the Dosen Kolundzija and now Sikirica, too; they all had these -- performed these acts of goodwill. For instance, a phone call. One such phone call is enough for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is enough, Dr. Lakcevic. I think you have given the three explanations. Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, let's forget about terminology for a moment. Do you agree that the guards who were deployed to Keraterm camp worked in shifts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many guards per shift?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 15 to 17 guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So having --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or ten; it depended. In other words, I cannot give you a precise figure, but somewhere within the range of ten to 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So, sir, the fact is that during these times, there was a hierarchical structure that ran through the police and was translated in practical terms at the Prijedor Police Station, and it was the Prijedor Police Station that deployed the guards in shifts to Keraterm camp. And in light, sir, of the tightening of the police structure, the police hierarchical structure at that time, surely, sir, among those guards in each shift there must have been someone who was in charge of the shift? That's the case, surely, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are no firm proofs for that. In fact, on the contrary. I assert that there are only guards because the police, as the executive organ, has to have strict rules, and this should have also been set out in the duty roster such as the one for the 5th and 6th of June. I believe --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let's put aside the rules for a moment. As a matter of common sense, as a matter of common police culture and practice, surely there must have been someone among those guards who was giving orders to the other guards and to whom the other guards would report? As a matter of common police sense, it follows, doesn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I cannot agree with you on that. First of all -- and I'll give you a very brief explanation why I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, I think you've given an explanation as to what your view was, and the point is, you disagree with me on that point. Let's move to another point. The role of those who were exercising security was -- you agreed on Thursday would include to protect the inmates and to ensure that they didn't escape. That's what you agreed with on Thursday, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You said also in your evidence on Thursday that they would play some kind of a role in terms of the arrest of the inmates. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they would play a role in the arrest of detainees. That I cannot say. I am certain that that I did not say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let me just see if I can assist your recollection. You said at point 12 on page 5438 of the transcript, you said this: "We have a report here indicating that the Omarska and Keraterm reception centres, in contravention of the usual practice, are constantly secured by the police officers. They are providing physical security to these facilities. In addition to this, they also carry out other tasks related to the arrests of person who are of interest for reasons of security." Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would now have to correct myself if that is indeed what I had stated, because people who are on security tasks were not there. In fact, I said that at first the military brought in about 600 inmates, and people who were on security tasks were not involved in bringing them over in -- or in releasing them from the Keraterm. If I had indeed said so, I must withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they play any part, that is, the guards in the camp, in terms of the interrogation of inmates that was going on in the camp?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This security detail is such that it cannot engage in even the simplest tasks such as -- such as gathering information pursuant to Article 151.1 of the law, because they do not know the procedures of conducting interviews, especially not such -- they have no psychological knowledge needed for such a subtle task. So they are no match for such types of tasks and did not engage in them. I also said that the teams were composed from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, and in the Prcac case, one of them actually detailed the method of how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. Putting aside the actual questioning that went on, did the guards play any role in terms of facilitating the interrogation? That is, for example, calling out those who were to be interrogated from a list and making sure that they were taken for interrogation. Did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a question that may require a two-part answer. First off that the team of investigators -- that the investigators from the team said themselves, "Please bring in the first five interviewees," or if this team from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre had some priority interviewees, then they may have asked for those. But he is only -- the guard is only following the orders of the superior; in other words, bringing in a particular person, meanwhile, all the time following the rules of -- that are the same for -- internationally, and it has to be a procedure that does not threaten the life or existence or health of an interviewee. But the fact that five persons were brought to be interviewed to one of the investigators' room in itself to me does not mean that there was any breach of rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What about the role of the guards in transferring the inmates, say, from Keraterm to Omarska or Trnopolje? I mean, they would be involved some way in effecting such a transfer, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules on public security, it is stated quite explicitly that persons guarding buildings and facilities cannot leave them. Therefore, I can assume that they were engaged only to the gate, up to the gate. And beyond the gate, it was other people. Also, these rules and regulations on guarding certain facilities explicitly state that such facilities cannot be abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just, by the way, on that point in terms of the transfer of prisoners from Keraterm camp, you gave some evidence on two occasions on Thursday to the effect that on the 27th of May, 1992, the Crisis Staff ordered that all prisoners from Keraterm were to be transferred to Omarska and that that, in fact, did take place. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I found that in documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And so it was your evidence that on the 27th of May, all of the prisoners from Keraterm were transferred to Omarska. And I think you even used the words, "I emphasise, all prisoners were transferred."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem. Could it be addressed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Sir, should I repeat the question for you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And so it was your evidence that on the 27th of May, all of the prisoners from Keraterm were transferred to Omarska, and I think you even used the words, "I emphasise, all prisoners were transferred." That was your evidence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that. As for this statement of mine, my testimony, it is based on evidence from the case itself that was made accessible to me. Whether this was actually carried out or not, that I cannot say. That is to say that I trusted the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So you relied on the document to conclude that, in fact, on the 27th of May, the prisoners were in fact transferred, that is, all of them, to Omarska. That's what you relied on.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So would it surprise you to learn that that, in fact, did not take place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be surprised. As a matter of fact, Defence counsel, Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Rodic, told me that it's a bit debatable whether it was that way then. However, I took this document -- what I'm trying to say is that this is supposed to be an answer to your question as well, and that is that, in a war situation, the relationship between a policeman and his superior becomes stricter. I mean, you asked me about this on Thursday. You asked me to explain what this order meant, a tightened situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, you are saying that his evidence was that all prisoners were, in fact, transferred on the 27th of May, or is it that his evidence was that according to the information that he had gathered from the documents that he read, all prisoners were to be transferred? One has to be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let me quote, if I could from the transcript. The question at page 5443 was this: "And on the basis of this decision --" it's referring to the Crisis Staff decision -- "did these prisoners of war later transfer to Omarska?"

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to this decision on 27 May, 1992, all, and I emphasise all, prisoners of war were transferred to Omarska. And then again at page 5448, the question was asked: "What did the Crisis Staff decide?"

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff decided to transfer all the detainees from Keraterm to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: On 27th May 1992, was this decision of the Crisis Staff implemented, that is, to transfer all the detainees from Keraterm to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the evidence you gave on Thursday. The question I'm asking you today is that is it your view that in fact on the 27th of May, all of the prisoners were transferred?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logically, linguistically, and legally, if we were to interpret the decision that way, then it would be the 27th, and I abide by this document. However, now it would be an illusion, and I don't see why that would be important, but then it's not for me to say, to say whether all were transferred or not. What is important here is what I already said by way of my expert opinion, and that is the question related to the accused Dosen and his role, whether he was a superior or not, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The point is that documents can be wrong. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. However, if one says the 27th and, due to certain circumstances, it could not be carried out then but, say, five days later, we have to take those circumstances into account, as well. However, probably through some report on the work of the Public Security Station of Sarajevo, this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of Prijedor, interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it should be noted that the prisoners were not transferred on the 27th but, say, on the 1st or 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you've gone as far as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let's get back to the role of the guards at the camp. It is, of course, fundamental that guards at the camp must not ill-treat the detainees themselves. That's fundamental, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that they cannot and should not disagree. I also mentioned the convention against terrorism which in article 10 states explicitly that all of those who interrogate certain persons, military personnel or police personnel, have to be trained for that. And I'm telling you now that work is being done on that, but before, it was not the case. The guards that were brought in to Keraterm, some guards that were brought in did not undergo any kind of police or security training. However, that does not give them the right as human beings to not act in a humane way towards persons who were detained in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Sir, under their duty, irrespective of their human inclinations, surely, sir, it's their duty not to ill-treat those whom they have in their care. Now, please, can you agree or disagree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And in accordance with their duty, they must not allow and, indeed, must prevent to the extent that they can any subordinate they may have from ill-treating any of the detainees. Can you agree or disagree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they do not have any subordinates. They did not have any subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Put aside that fact, assuming that they did have subordinates, you'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judgments are not based on assumptions. I have no comment, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. They're fairly basic tasks, in any event, aren't they, not to ill-treat detainees? It's a basic task. There's nothing complicated about it. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that they should not ill-treat persons who are in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is that there's nothing difficult or complicated about that duty, is there? It's a very basic, fundamental duty, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is so clear that there's no need to emphasise it, over-emphasise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: No. And there's certainly no need to have a security plan in place in order to carry out that duty, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has to be a security plan for other reasons, that is to say, to assess the security situation, the number of persons, et cetera, and within that framework, that which you are referring to right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not referring to the other reasons, I'm only referring to the duty not to ill-treat the detainees. That does not require any security plan in order to comply or implement that particular duty, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, the reserve police who were deployed at that time, that is, back in 1992, were drawn, I think you said, from two sources. Firstly, they were retired active policemen who had come back to perform certain duties, or they were persons who had been drawn from the military. They'd received -- persons who had military training; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right when you're saying that they were employed. That meant that they had a job, a permanent job. They were just assigned to the police station to carry out a certain kind of work. Also, I think that your question was taken out of the context of my expert opinion where I said how they were assigned. But I did not say at any point that there was a single retired policeman in Keraterm as a reserve policeman. As a matter of fact, I'm saying that all of those who were in Keraterm were outside the force and did not undergo any kind of training.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm just -- the point that I'm making is that those who were deployed, not necessarily in Keraterm but at that time, included those two categories; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that, what you said, because in the case of Prcac, he was a policeman. He was a forensic technician. And then when the conflict broke out, he became active again. But that's a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: That's a different matter, so we won't go down that track. But the point is that these -- these persons were actually paid for the work they did. So they were employed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That is a compensation they get instead of the salary, the wages they would get in a company. Or if they had no employment previously, then they're given compensation because they would be doing something as freelancers. However, we cannot use the word "employed," because "employed" means a person with full-time employment. Here he was assigned to security work. And that is also recognised in documents, please, that time spent on a reserve police force is considered as time spent on military drills and exercises. That's it. Even when working on security assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In any event, those that were there got money for what they did, for performing their duties. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They got money while they worked on security.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just getting back from -- getting back to where these people were drawn from, it's the case that they weren't just -- they wouldn't take just anyone. Anyone from the street could not just come and act as a reserve police officer at that time, could they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you. And this expression that you used, "from the street," it cannot be used that way, because this was a public manifesto, a public announcement that all able-bodied men of military age had to report. And then they reported, as specifically referring to Dosen, they reported at the local commune, that is, the lowest socio-political level - this is below the municipality - and then they assigned them. It was not from the street, because when people are engaged in security affairs there has to be a certain kind of order, a certain procedure. It has to be done in a certain way, and that's as it was here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You had to have been an active policeman who had had some service as an active policeman or you had to have done military training in order to become a reserve police officer. That's what you said in your report, sir. Agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in part. In part I agree. However, circumstances actually prevail, and it depends on the situation whether that will be observed or not. There is always an active policeman in Omarska and also a reserve policeman, and then that is a different professional situation. It did not exist here, though. The situation was such -- well, this is the way things were done. I'm not sure it absolutely had to be that way. I'm not sure whether there could have been a better organisation and whether active policemen could have been brought there as well, whether it could have been handled differently. However, we see that this Crisis Staff did decide that these should be men who then were assigned there ad hoc. And in order for me to be a reserve policeman, after doing my military service, I would have to be entered into the police structure, and I would have to gradually get appropriate training. The accused Dosen, and this also refers to Sikirica and Kolundzija, they did not go through this kind of training and they were not on these lists of reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The authorities accorded some weight to the fact that persons were -- had received military training. That appears to be the case. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, because -- actually, there is a document when Dosen did his military service. However, security culture belonging to the police, which involves a wide range of authority, should not be put into the hands of people who are inappropriately or insufficiently trained or educated. Generally speaking and also specifically from a police point of view, I've also said Dosen, Sikirica, and Kolundzija, had they refused to carry out a task, they would have been held accountable by a military court, and they would have been sentenced to more than the lady doctor who was sentenced to eight years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there. In terms of military training, anyone undertaking military training, and that would include the accused Damir Dosen, would be trained in the importance of correct treatment of civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part I could agree, because in the army, I am a soldier doing my military service, and I came to train in military activities. And in the army, this relationship is not defined to such an extent; that is to say, military interest is not represented in the police. The situation is different because, through communication with persons, there is interesting security information that is obtained and that is a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Sir, surely in military training, recruits, whatever they're called, would be trained in the proper treatment of civilians and indeed the proper treatment of prisoners. Agree or disagree, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say that military training is of decisive importance. As far as Dosen is concerned, I think that it is family upbringing that is more important, and we heard that he did certain things that were in the domain of goodwill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lakcevic, please answer the question that was asked. The question was, "Surely military training recruits, whatever they are called, would be trained in the proper treatment of civilians and, indeed, in the proper treatment of prisoners. Do you agree or disagree with that?" And let us just have a simple answer, not a discourse.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And can you just agree or disagree with some more propositions, please, without expanding unless you absolutely have to. They would also receive training in the use of weapons; agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were being trained. It's not that they passed certain examinations so that I could say whether they actually were trained or not. They were being trained. They were in the process of being trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. They would be trained in the importance of following orders and the importance of, in fact, giving orders; in other words, the importance of the army hierarchy, superior/subordinate army hierarchy. Would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the question is a leading one, and I don't think it's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not for you to determine. That is entirely out of order. It is for the Chamber to determine that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. May I just say one thing? I already answered in this respect that Dosen, Kolundzija, and Sikirica did not have the status, the official post of persons in superior positions -- persons of superior positions. So that's an answer to this question, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: All right. That's your answer, then. What about training in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Geneva Conventions? Did they receive some training in what the Geneva Conventions require?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'm referring to those persons who received military training. Did they get some training in the importance of respecting the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An ordinary soldier, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You know that Damir Dosen completed his military training and that he was, in fact, reportedly a very good soldier. You know that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you also know that he signed the solemn declaration which is Exhibit D26/2 in these proceedings. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, and I gave my comment concerning that in my expert opinion, what I think about the signing of the oath, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes, I'll come to that in a moment. But what flows, sir, from the fact that he was deemed or designated an authorised officer? What flows from that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorised official, including a reserve policeman in the case of emergency security, has the same treatment as a regular police officer de jure, but in practice, I think there is a wide discrepancy there. For instance, if Kolundzija were to come to Sikirica and they both had signed a solemn oath and are not professionally trained, and I do see that they had to have carried out the orders, the military type of orders, so if you -- if they showed their military ID, if they showed it to the person --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Please stop there. So on its face, the fact that the accused were designated an authorised officer gave the accused the same duties or power as an ordinary policeman; that's the effect of it. Would you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. In regard of Keraterm, yes, but outside of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in your report at page 12 that your view is that the solemn declaration signed by the accused Damir Dosen was a coerced declaration. That's what you said in your report. What I'm asking you is why you say that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I did not say coerced, but that is what it can be interpreted as because you will either sign it or you will be sent to the military tribunal. So he decided to sign it, which is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You never asked him why he signed it, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the position to interview Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So you just assumed that it must have been coerced. That's what you did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a general statement, and that is sort of what stands to reason, that the person who is not professionally trained is taken in to carry out a certain type of assignment, and I agree with that and what you stated. But there is some psychological coercion involved there which underlies his signing of the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In any event, sir, he signed the declaration, he was provided with a uniform and a weapon, he was certainly physically equipped to act as a policeman, and he worked alongside others who were similarly equipped, and he was paid to perform his tasks. Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And in addition, he had received military training and had been reportedly a very good soldier. What I'm suggesting to you, sir, is that having regard to all of those circumstances, the accused was, indeed, equipped to perform the very basic tasks that he was required to perform at Keraterm detention centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a clear enough question, Dr. Lakcevic. Can we have a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say yes as regard the physical security, but not more complex tasks within the police competences.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to some of the other tasks that he may have been required to perform at Keraterm. You gave some evidence on Thursday about the accused's responsibility for the conditions in the camp. Let me just see if I can have your responses to these questions. The accused in the camp would have some responsibility overseeing access to food and access to water that the inmates received. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because access to food, I don't -- it -- I don't find it clear enough what it means, access to food.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, if food was brought into the camp, wouldn't those who were guarding the inmates in the camp have some responsibility over who received access to that food and indeed to water in the camp?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be the case that those engaged in those duties would have some responsibility to ensure that injured prisoners received some treatment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duties would have been to inform the health centre by telephone or the police station commander, that is, the Prijedor II police station. And it could have been done cumulatively; in other words, both could have been informed. The Crisis Staff had organised the Keraterm camp and was duty-bound to organise and involve various subjects in order for this camp to be able to function in an organised way and fulfil its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the same would apply in terms of the guards allowing the inmates out of their rooms in order to receive fresh air and exercise; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept that in part. Any camp or prison clearly defines periods of time - two hours in some cases, some others may have different rules - for fresh air. In other words, it is prescribed to guards when, at what time they can let people out. And these are the so-called house rules that regulates distribution of food, when the food would arrive, and also other criteria such as sanitation, food, electrical power, water, and of course, medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just say there were no house rules. Wouldn't it be a basic function of the guards, if there were no house rules, to allow the inmates out of their rooms to receive some air and take some exercise?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Somebody within this structure has to designate how this issue of fresh air is to be regulated. My position is that somebody from the Prijedor II police station decided about the time period and the circumstances under which the doors to the rooms could be opened and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, you never saw such a designation, did you? You never saw such a document setting out what those house rules were, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I never saw it. But these rules could also be verbal ones. In other words, they could be verbal orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you were never privy to whether there were any verbal orders actually in existence, were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And, sir, wouldn't it be the case that if, say, the authorities provided inadequate food, then it would be the responsibility of the guards, in their ordinary duties, to allow visitors to come to the camp and bring food?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone who is superior to the guards has to decide on that. They themselves are risking -- I would agree with them as a humanist, but he would risk violating or clashing with the rules, the house rules or other regulations governing the facility. And I believe that it was Dosen, Sikirica, and Kolundzija, did such things, which I personally would have justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: But your personal view is that in doing such things, they in fact breached their duties. That was your view on Thursday. Is that still your view today?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think that, because in the police you have the principle of subordination, and the orders of the superior have to be carried out, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. provided they're not criminal acts. And the rules of behaviour has to be -- have been harmonised with other legislation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Sir, doesn't it seem odd to you that if the guards in the camp assisted the prisoners in terms of those very basic needs, that they would be in violation of their duties? Doesn't that seem quite bizarre to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing bizarre in times of war, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on, you gave some evidence about a document which is D39/2, which was a document issued or dated the 16th of July this year, which certifies that the accused Damir Dosen was engaged as a reserve policeman without any leading function. Do you recall that document and giving some evidence about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic is on his feet. Mr. Rodic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting my learned friend. Can we please see the document or can the witness please see the documents that he's asked to comment on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the document be shown. That's D39/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's just look at that document. It was issued at the request of the accused's attorney, and in the document, it says that, "It shall serve in the proceedings conducted before The Hague Tribunal and may not be used for any other purpose." I was wondering if you could assist us, sir, as to why that would be, why it couldn't be used for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia and in the current republics, the case is the same. The certificates issued are for very strictly defined purposes. So this was asked -- he -- the Defence counsel had made a request, and the police station commander did exactly like he was supposed to do. I think he did what was right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: But then why, sir, couldn't it be used for any other purpose except for entering into evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the counsel asked for the certificate for very strict purpose. In other words, if he was -- if it was used -- for instance, had Dosen been injured or something, then it would be then sent to the social care institutions for regulating his disability or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The other document that you gave some evidence about, which was Exhibit D20/2, was a document that was obtained in a similar fashion and is also dated the 16th of July, and it refers to Damir Dosen's role as a soldier. Do you remember that document? I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown that document. Can I have a look at that document? Is that D20/2?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You have D20/2 before you, sir. That's a document that refers to the accused Dosen's role as a soldier. Sir, that document, that is, D20/2, doesn't have the same restriction as the other document, does it? In fact, it says that, "The document has the character of a public document for the purposes of Article 171, paragraph 3, of the General Administrative Procedure Act and shall serve as a proof." That's what it says, that document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because here it states for proof, that means that Rade Aleksic, the chief -- and the Defence counsel may have omitted, they could have added for the -- providing evidence at The Hague Tribunal. In other words, The Hague Tribunal could have been added, but here it is -- it says evidence of proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know what turns on that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'll move along, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you've been going for some time. How much longer do you intend to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I intend to finish before or at the break, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let's go back again to the document D39/2, regarding the accused as a reserve policeman. That document doesn't refer to the birth date of the accused Damir Dosen, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't have access to that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can it be given back to him, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It doesn't refer to the birth date of the accused.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the military, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm asking you to look at the document that talks about his role as a reserve policeman, and it's quite simple: It doesn't refer to his birth date, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not. Do you need an answer why it doesn't?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: No, I don't need an answer why. It doesn't define the term "leading function," does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The leading function is not used.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It's not defined.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No leading function.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The question is, it doesn't say what a leading function is. It doesn't define the term "leading function," does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it should have been more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It doesn't refer to the accused's role in Keraterm camp at all, does it? Specifically, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: It refers to the Public Security Centre at Prijedor as the CJB when in fact at that time it was known as the SJB. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just sort of caught me off guard. Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of the Security Services was in Banja Luka, but this is the Public Security Centre. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And it does not reference the -- perhaps I'll rephrase that. It does not refer to any records that may have been used in preparation for the document, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Even though this is not usual, the usual practice, to say -- to quote what documents form the basis of this, but in that case, it would have been complete had it been referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Certainly on the other document dated the 16th of July, the records that were used in preparation for that document were referred to, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military is much more organised in that respect than the police in terms of issuing certificates and documents of that kind. In fact, such certificate is -- can -- forms -- this type of document can be bought as a form in military bookstores.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: All right, sir. But taking into account all of those factors that I've -- you've agreed with me on in relation to the role -- the document that refers to Damir Dosen's role as a policeman, you couldn't give it much weight, could you? Would you agree or disagree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, finally, sir, the commander of the police station at Prijedor was the person with the authority to punish subordinates in Keraterm camp who committed crimes or breaches of duty. That's your evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not hear you well. To whom does the right to punish refer? The security or -- to punish the security personnel, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The question was, sir, the commander of the police station at Prijedor was the person with the authority to punish subordinates in Keraterm camp who committed crimes or breaches of duty. That's your evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because according -- if we, if we have this physical security which is under the police commander, in our jurisdiction, not unlike in England, the police does not have the right to implement the provisions of criminal called law. They can only forward their complaint to the next level for investigation, and then it would be referred to the public prosecutor for instituting proceedings. So the commander of Prijedor II police station did not have the right to punish. He is duty-bound to report on a breach of discipline to the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The whole system of punishing those who breach discipline relied upon every particular officer in their particular position doing what they -- taking what reasonable measures they could in order to ensure that that -- the person who had committed the breach was indeed punished or disciplined. Would you agree with that general proposition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a small clarification. As I said, this is when it -- it refers to the active police officer on duty. That would be done by the security services centre, and the commander of the public security station would file such a report. However, because we have reserve police officers here, the punishment is not the same. The procedure is not the one that is applied to the regular officer. If the breach is more serious, such a police officer would be relieved of duty and would be referred to the military defence office, and as a rule, this office would send such a person to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Let me just put, finally, this proposition to you: The chain of reporting such breaches had to start with the one who observed the breach; correct? Because those superiors who were not there couldn't know about anything untoward unless they were told by those on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, are you going to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have about 15 minutes at the most, so I think we can proceed after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now. Dr. Lakcevic, we are going to adjourn for half an hour. We will resume at 11.30. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including the members of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lakcevic, I shall try to make my re-examination as short as possible, so I would kindly ask you for your cooperation. I shall put specific questions to you, and could you please keep your answers short as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for your conclusions during your testimony and also when you drafted your expert opinion, did you base them on documents and regulations concerning police work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that daily assignments of police work in the Prijedor II Police Station is the key document for the work of this police station for a given day. In practice, are the rights and rules of the shift commander, the deputy, the policeman, et cetera, are they all regulated in such a document or in laws?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They are not regulated by laws either. They are regulated by bylaws, and that is the rules on the internal organisation and job classification of the Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that document, it is precisely stated which facilities are provided with security and which members of the police take part in guarding these facilities. Is it necessary -- in this daily duty roster, is it necessary to describe their duties specifically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If there is a post of shift commander, do you agree with me that he should have greater responsibility than the other guards, and thereby it should be expected that such persons hold a higher rank within the police force, which would also be expressed by way of a higher salary in their favour?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to show the witness document D56/1 briefly. This is a payroll of the Prijedor II Police Station for the month of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you see the beginning of this document by the name and surname of -- names and surnames of the first three persons on that list, do you see the posts they hold? Please, just wait before answering. Can you tell us what these designations by the name mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mean, number one, Jokovljevic Ranko, deputy commander, it says ZK for smene komandir, that is, deputy commander; then Plavic Rajko, PK, that is, assistance commander, pomocnik komandir; then Grujic Boro, assistant commander, abbreviated as PK, pomocnik komandir. And also there's a difference in salaries. The deputy has 13.000, as far as I can see, and the two assistants have 11.000 respectively, whereas all others have 9.300 dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about inspectors, investigators, regardless of whether they belong to military or civilian security, state security, in the police hierarchy, are they considerably above policemen, especially ordinary policemen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly so. At least four or five steps are involved, to put this figuratively.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You already said that you used documents that were introduced by the Defence when giving your findings when you spoke about the 27th of May and the transfer of detainees from Keraterm to Omarska. Did you read this information in the report of the police station or, rather, the report of the Public Security Station of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that report it is said that on the basis of the decision of the Crisis Staff on the 27th of May, 1992, all prisoners of war were transferred to Omarska and then new ones were brought in, regardless of whether they were captured during armed conflict or were brought in on the basis of other operational procedures. Do you base your findings on these documents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, in the police report for the first six months published in June 1992, it was mentioned, inter alia, that the police guarded vehicles that transferred persons from Keraterm. In your opinion, as for this transfer, in addition to policemen, members of the reserve force of the Prijedor II police station, could the security have been provided by policemen from other police stations as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the arms and services where a military conscript does his military service, if such a person is later assigned in terms of his military obligation in -- is assigned to the military police, does this person have to undergo police training as well in order to know what legal authority he has as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is explicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for the accused Dosen, when he responded to his call-up, since he is a military conscript, was assigned to the reserve police force, is it customary in such a situation to sign the oath?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: First of all, had the accused Dosen not responded to the general mobilisation call-up, would he have to suffer certain sanctions because of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He would have been held criminally responsible by the law and criminal procedure, and this is a grave breach as it was carried out in times of war, and that would involve very severe punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Also during cross-examination, my learned friend from the Prosecution showed you a certificate that was issued by the police station Prijedor II in which it is stated that in the critical period of time, the accused Dosen did not have any leading duties or posts in the police. My question is the following: The information from this certificate, is it contained in the official records of the police station that issued that certificate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Also, the document that was issued by the Ministry of Defence, the military department in Prijedor, with all the information relating to the accused Dosen, his military service, the arms and services he belonged to during his military service, his ability to carry out military service in the military department, is there also a military file of his which is also an official document, an official record?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In conclusion, I would like to ask you one more thing. In keeping with legal regulations concerning police work, who gives orders concerning emergency security?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders concerning emergency security are issued by the head of the public security police station, in this case of Prijedor, or the commander of Prijedor II police station, because powers are transferred in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: One more question. A person who issues an order for emergency security, does such a person exercise control and supervision over how this emergency security is carried out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LAKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, such a person does so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just completed my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Dr. Lakcevic, that concludes your testimony, and you are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for everything. It was an honour for me to be here to answer questions, both those put by the Prosecution and those put by the Defence. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to take this opportunity to inform you that we have two more witnesses. One is a fact witness and the other one is an expert witness, a psychiatrist. So I would like to suggest that we first call the fact witness. I would not like to state this person's name publicly. I would kindly ask for protective measures; namely, I would like to ask for a pseudonym and for face distortion. Since this is a person who is an ethnic Muslim who lives in a third country, who for a certain period of time was in Keraterm, and for all these reasons, he has concerns for his own security and safety. So I would kindly ask the Court to grant him the protective measures that he is seeking. If you need any additional clarification or explanations, I stand ready to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The application is granted. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness will be Witness DR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the speaker. The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The microphone's on, but I wasn't speaking into it. There are one or two matters that I would like to raise with the Court at a convenient moment. They won't take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please move into closed session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there someone else with you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: There were two or three young men in the same car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where were you brought to exactly when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I was taken to the military police building behind the Keraterm building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us briefly what this building looked like?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: A small, like, prefabricated building with a few rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you questioned in this building?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I was questioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you were asked in that building?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: They asked me what my year of birth was, where I was born, my father's name, my mother's name, my name, where I was during the attack on Prijedor; things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what the man who interrogated you looked like?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I can't. There were a few men there, not only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did these men wear military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they perhaps have certain ranks?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I did not notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately the time when this happened, which month?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: The end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After the interrogation at the military police building, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I was taken to Room number 1 on the front side of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Approximately how much time did you spend in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Twelve days. On the twelfth day, I was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know a person nicknamed Kajin from before the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How well did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Well, as a man from town, nothing more than that. Just as Kajin, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever socialise with him or did you ever have any other kind of relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how your family found out that you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: When I came to Keraterm the first day, one of the guards walked up to me, and he said to me that he was my sister's schoolmate, and he said to me, "Do you want me to call your family and tell them where you are?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he ask you to make a phone call or what?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: No. He just asked me what the telephone number was, and he said that he would call my home, that he would call my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he actually did that?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After a few days, did you contact your family once again?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Two or three days later, yes. I actually rang my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Honourable Trial Chamber under which circumstances you made a telephone call to your home.

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: That day, Kajin walked up to me and said, "You want to ring your home?" And I said, "Yes, if I can." And he took me to some scales near the exit out of Keraterm, and that is where he gave me a telephone so that I could ring my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you actually phone your home? Who did you talk to and what was this telephone call about, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I talked to my mother, and I told her not to worry, not to be upset. And I told her to bring me some things and some food to Keraterm, some clothing and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you get something, any of these things that you asked your mother to send to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: During this time that I spent there, 11 days and the 12th day, on three occasions I got food and clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how these deliveries were made to you of the stuff that was sent to you by your family?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: My brother-in-law would bring it to the gate. He did it three times. And then from the gate, the guards would bring it to the room or in front of the room, and that was handed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Later on, did you learn whether everything that was sent to you actually reached you?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that had been sent to me reached me, including cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did other men who were detained in the same room with you also receive packages?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: They did. Not all of them, but some did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many people from among those of you who in that room at the time you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Seventy to 80 per cent of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you share what you received with other people who were detained with you there?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During this period of time that you spent in Keraterm, about ten days, you said, did you ever see Damir Dosen issuing any orders to anyone, either to the guards or to the people who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see Damir Dosen mistreat anyone, beat anyone, or attend beatings administered by others?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: No, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see Dosen talking to persons who were detained at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did these conversations look like, if you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: They were just regular conversations, and I noticed on a couple of occasions that they were laughing and making jokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the day when Keraterm was closed down?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened, based on your own recollection.

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: On that day, I don't know the exact number of buses that arrived and the police from the SUP in town, I don't know who was calling people out by names, but as we were being called out, they would proceed to board buses, and then we were bused to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these police from the Prijedor SUP involved in your transportation?

utterances.speaker: Witness DR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
